questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Calculate the vapour pressure that can help the formation of a spherical droplet of water of radius $6.25 \times 10^{-5}$ m at 22°C. Given: The surface tension of water at the given temperature is $7.28 \times 10^{-2}$ Nm^{-1}$.$
questions.solution:
The excess pressure inside a spherical droplet that helps in its formation is given by the formula:

$\Delta P = \dfrac{2T}{r}$

where $T$ is the surface tension and $r$ is the radius of the droplet.

Substituting the given values:
$T = 7.28 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{N m}^{-1}$
$r = 6.25 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m}$

$\Delta P = \dfrac{2 \times 7.28 \times 10^{-2}}{6.25 \times 10^{-5}}$

$\Delta P = \dfrac{14.56 \times 10^{-2}}{6.25 \times 10^{-5}}$

$\Delta P = 2.3296 \times 10^3\ \text{Pa}$

$\Delta P \approx 2.33 \times 10^3\ \text{Pa}$

Answer: $2.33 \times 10^3\ Pa$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small hollow vessel which has a small circular hole of radius r in its base, is immersed in a tank of oil of density $\rho$ and surface tension T. The oil will penetrate into the vessel at a depth of
questions.solution:
Let the depth at which the oil penetrates the vessel be $h$.

The hydrostatic pressure exerted by the oil at depth $h$ is given by $P = h\rho g$.

For the oil to enter the vessel through the small hole of radius $r$, this hydrostatic pressure must overcome the excess pressure due to surface tension at the meniscus formed at the hole.

The maximum excess pressure for a meniscus of radius $r$ is $\Delta P = \dfrac{2T}{r}$.

Equating the hydrostatic pressure to the excess pressure:

$h\rho g = \dfrac{2T}{r}$

$h = \dfrac{2T}{r\rho g}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2T}{r\rho g}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: While falling through the air, twenty seven droplets having the same radius 1 mm and terminal velocity $10 \mathrm{cms}^{-1}$ combine to form a single drop. What is the terminal velocity of the single bigger drop?
questions.solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of each small droplet and $R$ be the radius of the single large drop. Since the volume is conserved, we have $27 \times \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^{3} = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R^{3}$.

This implies $R^{3} = 27 r^{3}$, so $R = 3r$.

The terminal velocity $v$ of a droplet is given by Stokes' Law as $v = \dfrac{2}{9} \dfrac{r^{2} g (\rho - \sigma)}{\eta}$, where $\rho$ is the density of the liquid and $\sigma$ is the density of air.

From this expression, $v \propto r^{2}$.

Let $v_{1}$ be the terminal velocity of the small droplet and $v_{2}$ be the terminal velocity of the large drop. Then $\dfrac{v_{2}}{v_{1}} = \left( \dfrac{R}{r} \right)^{2}$.

Substituting $R = 3r$, we get $\dfrac{v_{2}}{v_{1}} = (3)^{2} = 9$.

Given $v_{1} = 10 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$, the terminal velocity of the larger drop is $v_{2} = 9 \times 10 = 90 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $90 \mathrm{cms}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Water from a tap emerges vertically downwards with an initial speed of $1.0 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. The cross-sectional area of the tap is $1 \mathrm{~cm}^2$. Assume that the pressure is constant throughout the stream of water and that the flow is steady. The cross-sectional area of the stream 15 cm below the tap is $\left(g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}\right)$
questions.solution:
Let the initial velocity at the tap be $v_1 = 1.0 \text{ ms}^{-1}$ and the cross-sectional area be $A_1 = 1 \text{ cm}^2$.

Let the velocity at a depth $h = 15 \text{ cm} = 0.15 \text{ m}$ be $v_2$ and the cross-sectional area be $A_2$.

Using the equation of motion $v_2^2 = v_1^2 + 2gh$, we have:

$v_2^2 = (1.0)^2 + 2 \times 10 \times 0.15 = 1 + 3 = 4$

$v_2 = 2 \text{ ms}^{-1}$

According to the equation of continuity for steady flow, $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$.

$1 \text{ cm}^2 \times 1.0 \text{ ms}^{-1} = A_2 \times 2.0 \text{ ms}^{-1}$

$A_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \text{ cm}^2 = 0.5 \text{ cm}^2$

Answer: $0.5 \mathrm{ cm}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In to a vessel containing pure water a clean glass tube of radius $3.6 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{ m}$ is held vertically with 12 cm of the tube above the water level. Now the capillary tube is moved down in to the water so that only 2 cm of its length is above the water surface. Angle of contact $\theta$ at this position is (given surface tension of water $=7.2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{Nm}^{-1}$ and $g=10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
The capillary rise $h$ in a tube of radius $r$ is given by the formula $h = \dfrac{2T \cos \theta}{r \rho g}$, where $T$ is the surface tension, $\theta$ is the angle of contact, $\rho$ is the density of water, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

First, calculate the maximum capillary rise $h_\max$ for pure water in a glass tube, where $\theta = 0^{{}^{\circ}}$ and $\cos 0^{{}^{\circ}} = 1$. Given $T = 7.2 \times 10^{-2} \text{ N/m}$, $r = 3.6 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$, $\rho = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$, and $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$h_\max = \dfrac{2 \times 7.2 \times 10^{-2}}{3.6 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000 \times 10} = \dfrac{14.4 \times 10^{-2}}{3.6 \times 10^0} = 4 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 4 \text{ cm}$.

When the tube is pushed down such that only $2 \text{ cm}$ is above the water surface, the water cannot rise higher than the top of the tube. The water will rise to the top of the tube, and the meniscus will adjust its curvature to satisfy the equilibrium condition $h' = \dfrac{2T \cos \theta}{r \rho g}$, where $h' = 2 \text{ cm}$.

Substituting the values: $2 \times 10^{-2} = \dfrac{2 \times 7.2 \times 10^{-2} \cos \theta}{3.6 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000 \times 10}$.

$2 \times 10^{-2} = \dfrac{14.4 \times 10^{-2} \cos \theta}{3.6} = 4 \times 10^{-2} \cos \theta$.

Therefore, $\cos \theta = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-2}}{4 \times 10^{-2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

This gives $\theta = 60^{{}^{\circ}}$.

Answer: $\theta=60^{{}^{\circ}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $A wooden block floats with \dfrac{3}{5}$ of its volume submerged in a tank of water. If a denser liquid is poured into the tank, the wooden block floats with half its volume in the liquid and the remaining half in water. The relative density of the liquid is:
questions.solution:
Let $V$ be the volume of the wooden block and $\rho_{w}$ be the density of water. Let $\rho_{b}$ be the density of the block and $\rho_{l}$ be the density of the denser liquid.

In the first case, the block floats in water. By the principle of flotation, the weight of the block equals the weight of the displaced water:

$\rho_{b} V g = \rho_{w} (\dfrac{3}{5} V) g$

$\rho_{b} = \dfrac{3}{5} \rho_{w}$

In the second case, the block floats in a mixture of water and the denser liquid. The total buoyant force equals the weight of the block. The block has half its volume in the liquid and half in water:

$\rho_{b} V g = \rho_{l} (\dfrac{1}{2} V) g + \rho_{w} (\dfrac{1}{2} V) g$

$\rho_{b} = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho_{l} + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho_{w}$

Substituting $\rho_{b} = \dfrac{3}{5} \rho_{w}$ into the equation:

$\dfrac{3}{5} \rho_{w} = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho_{l} + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho_{w}$

$\dfrac{1}{2} \rho_{l} = (\dfrac{3}{5} - \dfrac{1}{2}) \rho_{w}$

$\dfrac{1}{2} \rho_{l} = (\dfrac{6-5}{10}) \rho_{w} = \dfrac{1}{10} \rho_{w}$

$\rho_{l} = \dfrac{2}{10} \rho_{w} = \dfrac{1}{5} \rho_{w}$

The relative density of the liquid is $\dfrac{\rho_{l}}{\rho_{w}} = \dfrac{1}{5}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{5}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cylindrical tank 0.5 m in radius, rests on a platform 1.5 m high. Initially the tank is filled with water to a height of 2.5 m. A small plug whose area is $10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$ is removed from an orifice located on the side of the tank at the bottom. The vertical speed with which the water strikes the ground is: [Assume $g = 10 \text{ ms}^{-2}$]
questions.solution:
The orifice is on the side at the bottom, so water emerges horizontally with zero initial vertical velocity.

The platform height $H = 1.5$ m, so water falls 1.5 m vertically.

$v_y^2 = u_y^2 + 2gH = 0 + 2 \times 10 \times 1.5 = 30$

$v_y = \sqrt{30} \approx 5.47 \ ms^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hydraulic automobile lift is designed to lift cars with a maximum mass of 3000 kg. The area of cross-section of the piston carrying the board is $425 \mathrm{ cm}^2$. What maximum pressure would smaller piston have to bear?
questions.solution:
The maximum force, which the bigger piston can bear,
$F=30000 \mathrm{kgf}=3000 \times 9.8 \mathrm{ N}$
Area of piston,
$A=425 \mathrm{ cm}^2=425 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{ m}^2$
$\therefore$ Maximum pressure on the bigger piston,
$p=\frac{F}{A}=\frac{300 \times 9.8}{425 \times 10^{-4}}=6.92 \times 10^4 \mathrm{ Pa}$
Since, the liquid transmits pressure equally, therefore the maximum pressure the smaller piston can bear is $6.92 \times 10^4 \mathrm{ Pa}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Water flows from a tap with steady flow, through a cross sectional area of $10^{-3} \mathrm{ m}^2$ with a speed of $0.5 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$. Assume the pressure is constant throughout the stream of water. The cross sectional area of the stream $0.19 \mathrm{ m}$ below the tap is
questions.solution:
Let $A_1 = 10^{-3} \mathrm{ m}^2$ be the cross-sectional area at the tap and $v_1 = 0.5 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ be the speed of water at the tap. Let $A_2$ and $v_2$ be the cross-sectional area and speed at a depth $h = 0.19 \mathrm{ m}$ below the tap.

Using the equation of continuity, $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$.

Using Bernoulli's equation or the equation of motion for a freely falling body, $v_2^2 = v_1^2 + 2gh$.

Given $g = 9.8 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$ (or $10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$ depending on standard convention, here $9.8$ is standard), $v_2^2 = (0.5)^2 + 2 \times 9.8 \times 0.19 = 0.25 + 3.724 = 3.974$.

If we use $g = 10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$, $v_2^2 = 0.25 + 2 \times 10 \times 0.19 = 0.25 + 3.8 = 4.05$.

Taking $v_2 = \sqrt{4} = 2 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ (using $g=10$ and approximating $v_2^2 \approx 4$), we have $v_2 = 2 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$.

Substituting into the continuity equation: $A_2 = \dfrac{A_1 v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{10^{-3} \times 0.5}{2} = 0.25 \times 10^{-3} = 2.5 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{ m}^2$.

Answer: $2.5 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{ m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Modulus of rigidity of an incompressible liquid is
questions.solution:
The modulus of rigidity, also known as the shear modulus (G$), is defined as the ratio of shear stress to shear strain. For a fluid, shear stress is proportional to the rate of shear strain, not the shear strain itself. When a static shear force is applied to a liquid, it continues to deform indefinitely as long as the force is applied, meaning the shear strain is not defined for a static state. Consequently, the resistance to shear deformation in a liquid is zero. Therefore, the modulus of rigidity for any liquid, including an incompressible one, is zero.

Answer: Zero$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the relation obeyed by the angles of contact $\theta_1, \theta_2$ and $\theta_3$ of 3 liquids of different densities $P_1, P_2$ and $P_3$ respectively $(\mathrm{P}_1 < \mathrm{P}_2 < \mathrm{P}_3$) when they rise to the same capillary height in 3 identical capillaries and having nearly same surface tension $\mathrm{T}$ ?
questions.solution:
From Jurin's law: $h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{rPg}$

Since $h$, $T$, $r$, $g$ are constant: $\cos\theta \propto P$

Given $P_1 \lt P_2 \lt P_3$:

$\cos\theta_1 \lt \cos\theta_2 \lt \cos\theta_3$

Since liquids rise ($h \gt 0$), $\cos\theta \gt 0$, so all angles are acute: $0 \leq \theta \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

In $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, cosine is decreasing, so smaller cosine means larger angle:

$\theta_1 \gt \theta_2 \gt \theta_3$

Combined: $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \gt \theta_1 \gt \theta_2 \gt \theta_3 \geq 0$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: 64 rain drops of the same radius are falling through air with a steady velocity of $0.5 \mathrm{ cm} \mathrm{ s}^{-1}$. If the drops coalesce, the terminal velocity would be
questions.solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of each small drop and $v$ be its terminal velocity. The terminal velocity of a spherical drop is given by Stokes Law as $v = \dfrac{2}{9} \dfrac{r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{\eta}$, where $\rho$ is the density of the drop, $\sigma$ is the density of air, and $\eta$ is the coefficient of viscosity. This implies $v \propto r^2$.

When $n = 64$ drops coalesce into a single large drop of radius $R$, the volume remains constant. Thus, $\dfrac{4}{3} \pi R^3 = n \times \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3$, which gives $R^3 = n r^3$, or $R = n^{1/3} r$.

Substituting $n = 64$, we get $R = (64)^{1/3} r = 4r$.

Let $V$ be the terminal velocity of the large drop. Since $V \propto R^2$ and $v \propto r^2$, we have $\dfrac{V}{v} = \left( \dfrac{R}{r} \right)^2 = (4)^2 = 16$.

Given $v = 0.5 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$, the terminal velocity of the large drop is $V = 16 \times 0.5 \text{ cm s}^{-1} = 8 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

Converting to meters per second, $V = 8 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 0.08 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $0.08 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of wood floats in water with $(4 / 5)$ th of its volume submerged. If the same block just floats in a liquid, the density of the liquid is $\left(\right. in \mathrm{kgm}^{-3}$ )
questions.solution:
Applying Archimedes' principle, submerged part $=$ replaced water
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{4}{5} h \rho_{u s} g=h \times \rho_l \times g$
where, $\rho_w=$ density of water and $\rho_l=$ density of the liquid.
$\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore & \rho_l=\frac{4}{5} \times \rho_w=\frac{4}{5} \times 1000 \\
\Rightarrow & \rho_l=800 \mathrm{kgm}^{-3}
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The speeds of air-flow on the upper and lower surfaces of a wing of an aeroplane $arefv_1$ and $v_2$, respectively. If $A$ is the cross-sectional area of the wing and $\rho$ is the density of air, then the upward lift is
questions.solution:
Due to the specific shape of wings, when the aeroplane runs, air passes at higher speed over it as compared to its lower surface. This difference of air speeds above and below the wings, in accordance with Bernoulli's principle, creates a pressure difference, due to which an upward force called 'dynamic lift' acts on the plate.
$\therefore$ Upward lift $=$ pressure difference $\times$ area of the wings
$[\because F=p \times A]$
From Bernoulli's equation,
$\begin{aligned}
p_1+\frac{1}{2} \rho v_1{ }^2 & =p_2+\frac{1}{2} \rho v_2{ }^2 \\
\because \quad p_2-p_1 & =\frac{1}{2} \rho\left(v_1{ }^2-v_2{ }^2\right) \\
\text{ Hence, upward lift } & =\frac{1}{2} \rho A\left(v_1^2-v_2^2\right)
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Water from a tap of cross-sectional area $1 \mathrm{~cm}^2$, falls vertically downwards at $2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The cross sectional area of the stream, $20 \mathrm{~cm}$ below the tap is (assume that pressure is constant throughout and the flow is streamlined; $\left(\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}\right)$
questions.solution:
Let $A_1 = 1 \text{ cm}^2$ be the cross-sectional area at the tap and $v_1 = 2 \text{ m/s}$ be the velocity at the tap. Let $A_2$ be the cross-sectional area at a depth $h = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$ below the tap, and $v_2$ be the velocity at that point.

Using the equation of continuity, $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$.

Using the principle of conservation of energy (Bernoulli's equation) for a streamline, $v_2^2 = v_1^2 + 2gh$.

Substituting the given values, $v_2^2 = (2)^2 + 2 \times 10 \times 0.2 = 4 + 4 = 8$.

Thus, $v_2 = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2} \text{ m/s} \approx 2 \times 1.414 = 2.828 \text{ m/s}$.

From the continuity equation, $A_2 = \dfrac{A_1 v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{1 \times 2}{2\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ cm}^2$.

Calculating the value, $A_2 = \dfrac{1}{1.414} \approx 0.707 \text{ cm}^2$.

Answer: 0.707 cm^2

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A spherical metal ball of density '$\rho$' and radius '$r$' is immersed in a liquid of density '$\sigma$'. When an electric field is applied in the upward direction the metal ball remains just suspended in the liquid. Then the expression for the charge on the metal ball is :
questions.solution:
For the metal ball to remain suspended in the liquid, the net force acting on it must be zero. The forces acting on the ball are the gravitational force acting downwards, the buoyant force acting upwards, and the electric force acting upwards.

The gravitational force is $F_g = mg = V \rho g = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \rho g$.

The buoyant force is $F_b = V \sigma g = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \sigma g$.

The electric force is $F_e = qE$.

Equating the upward forces to the downward force:

$F_e + F_b = F_g$

$qE + \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \sigma g = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \rho g$

$qE = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 g (\rho - \sigma)$

$q = \dfrac{4 \pi r^3 (\rho - \sigma) g}{3 E}$

Answer: $q=\dfrac{\left[4 \pi r^3(\rho-\sigma) g\right]}{3 E}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The speeds of air-flow on the upper and lower surfaces of a wing of an aeroplane are $v_1$ and $v_2$, respectively. If $A$ is the cross-sectional area of the wing and $\rho$ is the density of air, then the upward lift is
questions.solution:
According to Bernoulli's principle for streamline flow, the pressure $P$ and velocity $v$ at any two points on a streamline are related by $P + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 = \text{constant}$.

Let $P_1 and P_2$ be the pressures on the upper and lower surfaces of the wing respectively, with corresponding air speeds $v_1 and v_2$.

Applying Bernoulli's equation:

$P_1 + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_1^2 = P_2 + \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v_2^2$

The pressure difference between the lower and upper surfaces is:

$P_2 - P_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho (v_1^2 - v_2^2)$

The upward lift force $F$ is the product of the pressure difference and the cross-sectional area $A$ of the wing:

$F = (P_2 - P_1) A$

$F = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho A (v_1^2 - v_2^2)$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}$ \rho A $\left(v_1^2-v_2^2\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of wood floats in water with $(4 / 5)$ th of its volume submerged. If the same block just floats in a liquid, the density of the liquid is (in $\mathrm{kgm}^{-3}$)
questions.solution:
Let $V$ be the volume of the block and $\rho_{w}$ be the density of water. Let $\rho_{b}$ be the density of the block and $\rho_{l}$ be the density of the liquid.

When the block floats in water, the weight of the block equals the weight of the displaced water:

$\rho_{b} V g = \rho_{w} V_{sub} g$

Given $V_{sub} = \dfrac{4}{5} V$, we have:

$\rho_{b} V g = \rho_{w} \left( \dfrac{4}{5} V \right) g$

$\rho_{b} = \dfrac{4}{5} \rho_{w}$

Taking the density of water $\rho_{w} = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^{3}$, we get $\rho_{b} = \dfrac{4}{5} \times 1000 = 800 \text{ kg/m}^{3}$.

When the block just floats in the liquid, the entire volume of the block is submerged, so the weight of the block equals the weight of the displaced liquid:

$\rho_{b} V g = \rho_{l} V g$

$\rho_{l} = \rho_{b} = 800 \text{ kg/m}^{3}$.

Answer: 800

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A raft of density $600 \mathrm{ g} / \mathrm{m}^3$ and mass $120 \mathrm{ kg}$ floats in water. How much weight can be put on the raft to make it just sink?
questions.solution:
The density of the raft is $\rho_{r} = 600 \text{ kg/m}^3$. The mass of the raft is $M = 120 \text{ kg}$.

The volume of the raft is $V = \dfrac{M}{\rho_{r}} = \dfrac{120}{600} = 0.2 \text{ m}^3$.

For the raft to just sink in water (density $\rho_{w} = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$), the total weight of the raft and the added mass $m$ must be equal to the buoyant force acting on the raft when it is fully submerged.

The buoyant force is $F_{B} = V \rho_{w} g = 0.2 \times 1000 \times g = 200g$.

The total weight is $(M + m)g = (120 + m)g$.

Equating the two, we have $120 + m = 200$.

Therefore, $m = 200 - 120 = 80 \text{ kg}$.

Answer: $80 \mathrm{ kg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Water is poured in a tank through a cylindrical tube of area of cross-section $A$ and ejecting water at a constant speed $4 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$. The tank contains a hole of area $\dfrac{A}{2}$ at bottom. Level of water in the tank will not go up beyond
questions.solution:
Let $A_{in} = A$ be the area of the inlet tube and $v_{in} = 4 \text{ m/s}$ be the velocity of water entering the tank. Let $A_{out} = \dfrac{A}{2}$ be the area of the hole at the bottom of the tank.

The level of water in the tank stops rising when the rate of water entering the tank equals the rate of water exiting the tank through the hole. This is the condition for steady state.

The rate of volume flow entering the tank is $Q_{in} = A_{in} \times v_{in} = A \times 4 = 4A$.

The rate of volume flow exiting the tank through the hole is $Q_{out} = A_{out} \times v_{out}$, where $v_{out}$ is the velocity of efflux given by Torricelli's law as $v_{out} = \sqrt{2gh}$, with $h$ being the height of the water level.

Equating the flow rates: $4A = \dfrac{A}{2} \times \sqrt{2gh}$.

Dividing both sides by $A$: $4 = \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{2gh} \Rightarrow 8 = \sqrt{2gh}$.

Squaring both sides: $64 = 2gh$.

Using $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$: $64 = 2 \times 10 \times h \Rightarrow 64 = 20h$.

$h = \dfrac{64}{20} = 3.2 \text{ m}$.

Answer: $3.2 \mathrm{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: According to Pascal's law, pressure in a fluid at rest is the same at all points, if
options: they are at the same plane
they are at the same height
questions.solution:
Pascal's law states that for a fluid at rest, the pressure at all points at the same horizontal level is identical. In a continuous fluid at rest, the pressure variation with depth is given by $P = P_0 + \rho gh$, where $h$ is the depth measured from the surface. Points at the same vertical height (or same plane) have the same depth $h$, and therefore experience the same pressure.

Answer: they are at the same height

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The surface tension of a liquid at its boiling point
options: is equal to the value at room temperature
is half of the value at room temperature
questions.solution:
Surface tension is a property of liquids that arises due to the cohesive forces between molecules at the surface. As the temperature of a liquid increases, the kinetic energy of the molecules increases, which weakens the intermolecular forces of attraction.

At the boiling point, the liquid is in equilibrium with its vapor phase. The density of the liquid phase decreases while the density of the vapor phase increases as the temperature approaches the critical temperature. At the critical temperature, the distinction between the liquid and vapor phases disappears, and the surface tension becomes zero.

For any liquid, as the temperature reaches its boiling point, the surface tension decreases significantly. Specifically, at the critical temperature, it vanishes. In the context of standard physics problems, the surface tension of a liquid at its boiling point is considered to be zero.

Answer: becomes zero

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball floats on the surface of water in a container exposed to the atmosphere. When the container is covered and the air is partially removed, then the ball
options: remains immersed at its former depth
questions.solution: In the given situation, the weight of the ball is supported by the buoyant force of water and buoyant force due to air. As the density of air becomes less, the buoyant force due to the air becomes less. Therefore, to compensate a greater buoyant force due to water is required which is achieved by a greater immersion of ball into the water.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A frame made of metallic wire enclosing a surface area $A$ is covered with a soap film. If the area of the frame of metallic wire is reduced by $50 \%$, then the energy of the soap film will be changed by
questions.solution:
Given, initial surface area, $A_{1}=A$
Final surface area, A_{2}=A_{1}-50 \% of $AA_{2}=A-50 \% of A=A-\frac{A}{2}=\frac{A}{2}$ Initial surface energy, $E_{1}=T \cdot 2 A=2 T A$ Final surface energy, $E_{2}=$ Surface tension $\times$ Surface $\Rightarrow \quad E_{2}=T \times 2\left(A_{1}-A_{2}\right)=T \times 2\left(A-\frac{A}{2}\right)\Rightarrow \quad \quad E_{2}=T A\therefore$ Percentage change in the energy of soap film $\begin{aligned}$&=$\frac{E_{1}-E_{2}}{E_{1}} \times100 \\ \text{$ and $} =\frac{2 T A-T A}{2 T A} \times100 \\ \text{ and } =50 \%
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A fluid is in streamline flow across a horizontal pipe of variable area of cross-section. For this which of the following statements is correct?
options: Velocity of fluid is maximum at narrowest part.
Pressure of the fluid is maximum at widest part.
questions.solution:
According to the equation of continuity, A v=$\text{ constant }$ Therefore, velocity of the fluid is minimum at the widest part and maximum at the narrowest part of the horizontal pipe.
Again, according to Bernoulli's principle for horizontal pipe, p+$\frac{1}{2}$ p v^{2}=$\text{ constant }$ Hence, $p$ is more, $v$ is less and vice-versa.

questions.q: From the adjacent figure, the correct observation is
options: the pressure on the bottom of tank (I) is greater than at the bottom of (II)
the pressure on the bottom of tank (I) is smaller than at the bottom of $(I)$
the pressure depend on the shape of the container
the pressure on the bottom of (I) and (II) is the same
questions.solution:
The pressure applied at the bottom of a container by a liquid column of height $h$ is given by
$p=h \rho g$
Here, in two cases, the liquid used is same (water), so $\rho$ is same. Also, the height of liquid column is same on both. So, the pressure applied at the bottom is same for both.

questions.q: If a liquid does not wet glass, its angle of contact is
questions.solution: If a liquid does not wet glass, it means that the liquid-liquid interaction (cohesion) is more than liquid - solid interaction (adhesion). So, the angle of contact is obtuse.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: With the addition of impurities, surface tension of a liquid
options: may increase or decrease depending on impurities
questions.solution:
The addition of impurities in a liquid may increase or decrease the surface tension of liquid depending on the nature of impurities.
If the impurities are highly soluble in liquid, then it will increase the surface tension. But if it is less soluble in liquid, then it will decrease the surface tension of liquid.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A soap bubble of radius $r$ is blown up to form a bubble of radius $3 r$ under isothermal conditions. If $\sigma$ is the surface tension of soap solution, then the energy spent in blowing is
questions.solution:
Surface area of bubble of radius, $r=4 \pi r^{2}$
Surface area of bubble of radius, $3 r=4 \pi(3 r)^{2}=36 \pi r^{2}$
Therefore, increase in surface area =36 \pi r^{2}-4 \pi r^{2}=32 \pi r^{2} Since, a bubble has two surfaces, the total increase in surface area $=2 \times 32 \pi r^{2}=64 \pi r^{2}\therefore$ Energy spent $=$ Work done $=$ Surface tension \times Total increase in surface area $=64 \pi \sigma r^{2}$

questions.solution:
As, radius of bigger drop, $R=n^{1 / 3} r=2^{1 / 3} r \begin{aligned}&\Rightarrow R^{2}=2^{2 / 3} r^{2} \Rightarrow \frac{r^{2}}{R^{2}} \text{$ or $}2^{-2 / 3} \\
&\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{ Initial surface energy }}{\text{ Final surface energy }}&=\frac{2\left(4 \pi r^{2} T\right)}{ \left(4 \piR^{2} T\right)}=2\left(\frac{r^{2}}{R^{2}}\right)\\
&=2 \times2^{-2 / 3}=2^{1 / 3} \text{ or }2^{1 / 3}: 1
\end{aligned}
